QF.id: AIFM Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Market Theory_8

question.text: A fund manager at Yamuna Multi-Asset AIF is evaluating adding one of four new strategies to the existing portfolio. The correlation of each candidate with the current portfolio is: Strategy W: +0.50; Strategy X: +0.10; Strategy Y: -0.20; Strategy Z: -0.75. Which strategy offers the HIGHEST diversification benefit?

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Chapter 4.8 states: 'Lower the correlation, higher the benefits of diversification.' A correlation of -0.75 is the lowest (most negative) of the four, so Strategy Z maximises risk reduction when combined with the existing portfolio. At ρ = -1 the theoretical risk-elimination is complete. **The Trap:** W at +0.50 actually amplifies covariance. X at +0.10 offers modest benefit. Y at -0.20 helps more than X but less than Z. Candidates who 'fear negative' often pick X — that is the trap. **Cross-Exam Context:** Identical sample question appears in Chapter 4 of the XIX-C workbook itself and in XXI-B / XV. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** On paper, a negatively-correlated AIF sleeve (say long-volatility Cat III) looks ideal alongside a Cat II PE book. But negative correlation in stress scenarios often breaks down ('all correlations go to 1') — stress-test in the IC deck, don't just cite historical ρ.
